street_smart.title: You book a cab or auto through a ride app. Minutes before pickup, the driver calls and asks you to cancel the app booking and instead pay him directly in cash for a 'better rate' for the same ride. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: No single incident in today's feeds fits this cleanly, so it rotates in from the evergreen list: auto/cab overcharging & refusal. This specific mechanism (drivers steering riders off-app before the trip) hasn't been the street-smart scenario in the last three weeks — the closest recent entries were an in-ride fare-doubling dispute (2026-08-03, outside the 3-week window) and an accident-support angle (2026-08-14, a different mechanism).
street_smart.situation: You're standing outside your building waiting, it's raining, and the driver sounds friendly and reasonable on the call.

choices.text: Decline and ask him to keep the trip on the app as booked — if he won't, cancel and book a fresh ride.
choices.feedback: Correct. Staying on the app keeps your trip logged with a route, driver ID, fare record and live tracking that you can share or dispute later. Off-app cash rides have none of that — if there's a fare dispute, an accident, or anything goes wrong during the ride, you have no record and no platform support to fall back on.

choices.text: Agree, since a lower cash fare sounds like a good deal and it's raining outside.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Drivers who ask you to cancel and pay cash are usually trying to dodge the platform's commission — but once you're off the app, the 'better rate' often turns into a higher fare mid-ride, with no booking record to fall back on, no route tracking for your safety, and no way to file a complaint with the platform afterward.

choices.text: Agree to the cash rate, but note down the vehicle number yourself before getting in.
choices.feedback: Better than nothing, but a vehicle number alone doesn't get you fare protection, live-location sharing, or a formal complaint channel — the platform can't help with a ride it has no record of. If something goes wrong, you're relying entirely on your own note and memory.

choices.text: Ignore the call and just wait to see if the driver shows up for the original app booking anyway.
choices.feedback: The driver may simply cancel the trip from his end once you don't respond, leaving you stranded in the rain with no ride and having to rebook from scratch. It's better to explicitly tell him to keep it on the app, or cancel and rebook yourself right away.

takeaways: A driver asking you to cancel an app booking for a cash 'deal' is a common way to dodge platform commission — it usually costs you more, not less, once you're off-record.
Only your ride app's trip history counts as proof of the fare, route and driver — verbal cash agreements leave you with nothing to dispute later.
If a driver pushes hard to go off-app, it's simplest to cancel and book a new ride rather than argue on a call before you've even gotten in the vehicle.

quiz.question: In India's banking system, what does the 'repo rate' refer to?
options: The rate at which RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks
The interest rate banks pay on savings accounts
The GST rate applied to gold purchases
The exchange rate between the rupee and the dollar
quiz.why: The opposite rate — where RBI borrows from banks — is called the reverse repo rate; both are key tools the RBI uses to control inflation and liquidity.
